idiom_name: function literals (closures) over the method's locals; struct with methods when the state must be named
implementation_notes: Go function literals are closures: they may refer to variables of the surrounding function, and those variables are shared - not copied - and survive as long as they are accessible (Go spec), so the extracted steps become closures over one set of locals. A method value (o.Method) binds a receiver into a function value, which is the other half of the method-object idea. Promote the closure set to a struct with methods, passing the state as the receiver, as soon as the algorithm needs more than one operation or the state must be documented, reset or shared across requests; keep closures for small pipelines.
pitfalls: Go captures the variable, not its value: every closure shares the same storage, so a closure stored on a long-lived struct keeps the captured object alive and re-reads it on every call.
Before Go 1.22 the loop variable was shared between iterations, so closures created in a loop all observed the final value; go vet's loopclosure check reports the pre-1.22 module case.
Taking a method value repeatedly in a hot path allocates a closure carrying the receiver, and a value-receiver method value copies the receiver at binding time.
